nameStory: The Karner blue butterfly gets its name from Karner, New York, a small town halfway between Albany and Schenectady where it was first discovered in the Albany Pine Bush. This tiny blue jewel was actually first identified and described by the famous novelist Vladimir Nabokov, who was also a passionate lepidopterist (butterfly scientist).
description: The Karner blue is a small, delicate butterfly with wings that span only about an inch across. Males display brilliant silvery-blue wings that shimmer in sunlight, while females are more subdued with grayish-brown wings often touched with blue at the base. Both sexes have small orange crescents and black spots decorating the undersides of their wings, creating intricate patterns that look almost like tiny works of art.

idTips.label: Male wing color
idTips.description: Males have bright silvery-blue upper wings that catch and reflect sunlight with an almost metallic shimmer

idTips.label: Female wing color
idTips.description: Females display grayish-brown wings, sometimes with blue coloring near the wing base, giving them a more muted appearance than males

idTips.label: Wing underside pattern
idTips.description: Both sexes show pale gray undersides decorated with small black spots ringed in white and a row of orange crescents along the wing edges

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small butterflies with wingspans of about one inch, appearing delicate and almost fairy-like in flight

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies low to the ground with a fluttering, bouncing motion rather than smooth gliding

idTips.label: Lupine association
idTips.description: Almost always found near wild blue lupine plants, which have distinctive palm-shaped leaves and tall spikes of blue-purple flowers

habitat: Karner blues live in sandy, open areas like pine barrens, oak savannas, and prairie edges where wild blue lupine thrives. In New England, you'll find them mainly in southern New Hampshire's sandy soils and similar habitats with scattered trees and plenty of sunlight. They need areas that experience occasional natural disturbances to maintain the open conditions that both the butterfly and its host plant require.

seasonality.spring: The first generation emerges in late May when wild blue lupine begins blooming, with males appearing slightly before females.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs in early June, then again during the second generation from mid-July through mid-August when you'll see fresh butterflies nectaring on flowers.
seasonality.fall: Adults disappear by late August, though caterpillars may still be found feeding on lupine leaves before overwintering.
seasonality.winter: No adults present; the species overwinters as tiny caterpillars hiding among lupine plants and leaf litter.

funFact: This butterfly was immortalized in literature before it was even officially named - Vladimir Nabokov wrote about 'a score of Karner blues' in his novel Pnin, describing them without using their scientific name, years after he had discovered and classified the species himself.
confusionNotes: The Karner blue can be confused with other small blue butterflies like the Northern blue, but Karner blues are almost exclusively found near wild blue lupine plants. If you don't see lupine nearby, you're probably looking at a different species - this is your best field clue since Karner blue caterpillars can only survive on lupine.
contextualKnowledge: The Karner blue is New Hampshire's official state butterfly and is federally endangered, making any sighting special and worth reporting to local naturalists. It's one of the few butterflies discovered and named by a famous novelist, highlighting the intersection of science and literature in natural history.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Northern blue, the Karner blue is slightly smaller and has a stronger dependence on sandy habitats with wild blue lupine. Northern blues are more habitat-generalist and can use various legume plants as hosts, while Karner blues are lupine specialists. The wing patterns are quite similar, so habitat and host plant associations are often more reliable identification features than wing markings alone.
